title: Validator‑Guided Repair on a Shared Initial LLM Candidate: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation for Network Configuration Safety
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) to measure the downstream effect of a deterministic network‑configuration validator plus an allowed single automated repair on the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Using the declared generator gpt‑5‑mini (hosted adapter label openai_responses) and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on N = 200 paired intents (completed_episode_count = 400; model_calls_used = 200), every shared initial candidate passed validator checks so no repairs were attempted or applied (repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0). Observed outcomes: baseline_success = 200/200, guarded_success = 200/200; paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0, 0.0]. We provide artifact‑grounded methodology, representative validator diagnostics, reconciliation statistics, and a focused discussion clarifying the causal limits of the executed estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics and preregistered follow‑on designs required to measure repair efficacy under independent sampling or adversarial conditions.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being evaluated as intent→configuration translators in network operations (NetOps). Erroneous or hallucinated device commands can cause availability loss, policy violations, or other operational harm when applied. A commonly proposed mitigation is a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline: produce a candidate configuration, deterministically validate it against intent, topology and workflow constraints, and apply automated repairs when the validator detects violations. Prior work shows verifier‑guided feedback improves correctness in related domains (e.g., infrastructure‑as‑code) but does not directly establish transfer of those gains to device‑level execution with packet‑level fidelity. The present study measures a narrowly defined estimand: the causal effect of applying a deterministic validator and at most one automated repair to an identical sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). By design, sampling variability between baseline and guarded arms is removed, so any paired difference must arise from downstream validation/repair applied to the identical candidate. This narrow causal identification clarifies the role of validator‑triggered repair but does not evaluate independent sampling, prompt engineering, or multi‑model generality.
sections.related_work: Three literature streams motivate the experiment. First, surveys and empirical analyses document hallucination and factuality problems in LLM outputs and motivate grounding/verification strategies for operational tasks [1]. Second, retrieval‑augmented and evidence‑grounded pipelines reduce hallucination in operations‑style QA but typically evaluate textual correctness rather than device‑level executability [2]. Third, verifier‑guided generate→verify→repair architectures (e.g., recent IaC tools) report accuracy improvements in code/infrastructure generation and program repair domains; these studies motivated our use of a deterministic validator and a single automated repair attempt, but the supplied literature does not present standardized execution‑level device emulation results for NetOps [3]. Surveys of AIOps and NetOps benchmarking highlight heterogeneous task scopes and the absence of an established execution‑level safety benchmark in packet‑level simulation, further motivating a precise preregistered small‑scale empirical study with strong artifact provenance [4]. Our work complements these streams by operationalizing a reproducible paired estimand and reporting artifact‑grounded diagnostic evidence explaining why the repair stage did or did not alter outcomes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered prior to any model calls (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01; preregistration SHA‑256: f0c8330d3d74cb95461d3f0291ba1b607c427ad37b5edc3750cad593bd4aae76). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics (each intent produced exactly one sampled generation reused by both arms). Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline (validator + ≤1 repair) reduces the rate of executable unsafe configurations relative to baseline on the same sampled candidate. Planned confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar; alpha = 0.05. Power planning targeted an absolute risk reduction of 10 percentage points for N = 200 pairs.

Task bank, contamination defense, and selection. A deterministic task generator produced a fixed manifest of 200 synthetic "intent_configuration_repair_v1" tasks. Each task artifact records initial_state, required_sequence, difficulty annotations (e.g., "safe_access_service_transfer", "rolling_access_vlan_migration"), and a generation_seed for deterministic replay. The preregistered contamination procedure (SHA‑256 exact‑match plus n‑gram similarity checks) flagged no exact matches and therefore no confirmatory exclusions. Contamination summaries and the task manifest are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; analysis/contamination_summary.csv).

Generation semantics, model configuration, and sampling. Execution used the declared generator gpt‑5‑mini via the hosted adapter openai_responses; execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini" and temperature = null (unset). We explicitly note that temperature = null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; nondeterministic sampling remains possible. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, consistent with a single shared sampled candidate per pair as preregistered. The provider audit further records cache_hit_count = 0 and cache_miss_count = 200.

Validator and repair policy. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation". The validator deterministically parses candidate command sequences, maps them against the task's required_sequence, workflow_policies, and protected interface constraints, and produces structured traces (validation_before, validation_after, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes). For guarded episodes a single automated repair attempt was permitted (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Repair provider traces (when produced) and validator traces are archived under execution/scoring/*.json. The analysis maps validator.valid = true to a binary 'executable and compliant' label used in the paired test.

Execution accounting and missingness rules. The preregistered sampling plan fixed N = 200 intents and allowed up to two episodes per pair (baseline + guarded), planned_episode_count = 400. Missingness policy used the 'complete_pair_primary' rule: exclude incomplete pairs where either episode is missing; sensitivity analysis 'failure_as_zero' treats missing or failed episodes as unsafe. The final analysis reports complete pair accounting, failure counts, and reconciliation artifacts. All execution and reconciliation artifacts are archived and hashed per the manifest.
sections.results:
Execution and reconciliation. The execution manifest shows planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared sampled generation per pair), and complete_pairs = 200. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirm episode accounting, the provider audit, and the absence of cross‑condition cache reuse beyond the intended shared generation stage.

Primary outcomes and inferential summary. Validator mapping yielded baseline_successes = 200/200 and guarded_successes = 200/200 (analysis/condition_summary.csv). The observed paired contingency table is: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The exact McNemar two‑sided test produced p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the paired difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) is [0.0, 0.0] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). These results are artifact‑consistent: the single shared candidate per pair was judged validator.valid = true for every pair, so the guarded pipeline never had an opportunity to repair.

Repair activity and representative diagnostics. Across the confirmatory sample repair_attempt_count = 0 and repair_applied_count = 0. Representative per‑episode JSON artifacts (examples archived in execution/scoring/, e.g., task‑000004‑baseline.json and task‑000004‑guarded.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate text and identical validation_after.normalized_configuration values for baseline and guarded. Example normalized candidate excerpt for task‑000004: "interface edge2 admin down\ninterface edge2 vlan 40\ninterface edge2 admin up\ninterface edge1 admin down" with parsed_command_count = 4 and required_command_count = 4 and validator.valid = true. Table 2 (below) summarizes representative diagnostics for selected high‑difficulty tasks; full per‑task validator traces are archived.

Contamination and provider audit. Preexecution contamination checks flagged no exact matches (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). Provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200, stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200. All deterministic consistency checks passed (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Interpretation of degenerate contingency. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the only causal mechanism by which guarded could differ from baseline is validator detection followed by repair applied to the identical candidate. Because no shared sampled candidate triggered a validator violation, the guarded pipeline could not alter outcomes and the paired difference is necessarily zero. Thus the executed estimand provides evidence only about validator/repair effects conditioned on the observed shared samples and task bank—not about repair efficacy under independent sampling, adversarial uplift, or changes to generator sampling parameters.
sections.discussion:
Causal scope and implications. The shared_initial_candidate design isolates downstream validator/repair causal effects by removing sampling variability between arms. This internal clarity comes at the cost of external breadth: the experiment does not measure whether a guarded pipeline reduces the frequency of unsafe first‑pass generations when sampling independently per condition, nor whether constrained prompting or temperature control would change first‑pass validity. Consequently, the null paired difference must be read as an estimand‑specific null: the GVR pipeline did not affect outcomes because the validator found no faults in any sampled candidate.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: design intentionally eliminated per‑condition sampling differences; internal attribution of any downstream repair effect remains valid but is vacuous here because no repairs occurred. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces an explicit mapping from intent constraints to checks (syntax, sequencing, protected interfaces) and returns detailed traces; however the validator is an abstraction and does not execute vendor CLI or run packet‑level emulation. External validity: a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini via openai_responses), a synthetic task bank, and one validator were used; generalization to other models, task distributions, or higher‑fidelity validators is unsupported by the archived artifacts. Conclusion validity: the absence of discordant pairs yields no information about repair effectiveness under alternative designs.

Operational and experimental follow‑ons supported by archived artifacts. Using the same task bank, provider audit logs, and validator interfaces we preregistered concrete follow‑on estimands that would exercise the repair path: (A) independent per‑condition sampling (remove shared_initial_candidate) to let the guarded arm see separate first‑pass samples; (B) difficulty or adversary uplift by selecting 'extreme' difficulty tasks or injecting adversarial perturbations to increase validator failure rates; (C) explicit sampling control by setting non‑null temperature values and preregistering temperature sweeps to study the diversity vs validator‑failure tradeoff; (D) validator fidelity uplift by integrating vendor CLI semantics and packet‑level emulation so repairs are evaluated against runtime behavior; and (E) multi‑model sampling to assess generator heterogeneity. Each follow‑on design requires revised preregistration (different estimand and inferential plan) but can reuse the archived task manifest and reconciliation artifacts.

Why artifact grounding matters for interpretability. The archived per‑episode JSONs include validation_before/after subtables with parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and repair_applied flags. These artifacts make transparent why repairs did not execute: for every pair the validator.valid flag was true before any repair attempt. The model_configuration.json explicitly records declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini" and temperature = null; as required, null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling. The master prompt immutable reference and preregistration SHA are included in the archive to support reproducibility and independent audit.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory experiment that measured the causal effect of deterministic validation and an allowed single automated repair on the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). With gpt‑5‑mini declared as the generator and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the scorer, every shared initial candidate passed validation and no repairs were attempted or applied; guarded and baseline outcomes were identical for the executed estimand (paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This artifact‑grounded null result illustrates an estimand boundary: under shared_initial_candidate semantics and the sampled synthetic task bank, the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to change outcomes. It does not imply that GVR pipelines are unnecessary in general. Preregistered follow‑on experiments that (1) remove shared_initial_candidate semantics, (2) increase task difficulty or inject adversarial inputs, (3) set explicit sampling parameters, and (4) raise validator fidelity are required to evaluate repair efficacy under realistic sampling variability and adversarial conditions. All execution, analysis, and reconciliation artifacts referenced in this paper are archived to enable exact reproduction of the executed estimand and to support precise preregistered extensions.

Declared model used in execution: gpt‑5‑mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (model_calls_used = 200; execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Generation semantics executed: shared_initial_candidate — exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded conditions (no independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling). Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored candidates using 'full_intent_constraint_validation' and a single automated repair iteration was permitted in guarded episodes; in this run the validator flagged no violations and no repairs were applied (repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0). Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired intents) completed without preregistration deviations; execution and analysis artifacts are archived under execution/* and analysis/*. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence in this final run. After the autonomy lock no human manually rewrote technical results, manuscript text, figures, or references.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design produced exactly one sampled initial generation per intent and reused it across baseline and guarded conditions; this measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition sampling or prompt engineering.

Temperature unset (temperature = null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt‑5‑mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' items and the deterministic validator is an abstraction; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed on live devices.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects the task bank and sampling semantics rather than evidence that GVR is unnecessary in general.
